11        Mr. Taylor, I describe the development of the proposed revenue distribution among

15        consideration of increases that are somewhat higher or lower than the system

 1                    IV.    REVENUE INCREASE DISTRIBUTION

 2   Q.   What topic do you discuss in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   I describe SPS’s proposed methodology for distributing the proposed revenue

 4        increases among the customer classes.

 5   Q.   What principles have you relied upon in deciding how to distribute the

 6        proposed revenue increases among the customer classes?

 7   A.   The main consideration when balancing the distribution of the base rate revenue

 8        increase is the overall effect from the CCOSS-based increase in customer class

 9        revenue recovered through base rates combined with other charges, including fuel

10        and purchased power costs, renewable portfolio standard costs, energy efficiency

11        costs, electric vehicle infrastructure costs, and grid modernization costs. Reaching

12        a reasonable balance among those considerations is a matter of judgment and can

13        involve considerable discussion among customer groups with diverging interests,

14        in reducing a rate increase while allowing SPS the opportunity to recover the cost

15        of providing safe and reliable service during a period of transition for industry. My

16        consideration has the following results:

17          (1) the proposed ROR for individual classes will generally move closer to the
18              system average ROR;

19          (2) Irrigation Service and Primary General Service customer classes provide
20              funding for the proposed gradualism adjustment to other customer classes,
21              yet their proposed increases are lower than the overall average 16.7%
22              proposed New Mexico retail increase in total revenue; and

 1          (3) the proposed base rate increases for customer classes will range from 100%
 2              to 150% of the base rate increase on total New Mexico retail revenue
 3              including fuel and purchased power charges, renewable portfolio standard
 4              charges, and energy efficiency charges.

 5   Q.   Why does SPS’s proposed revenue distribution not move each class to the same

 6        ROR?

 7   A.   The CCOSS represents the expected composition of costs and customers, including

 8        their associated energy usage and demands, for the FTY. However, while the

 9        CCOSS contains a high level of data and is the result of the analysis of that data,

10        other factors can be considered when determining what level of forecasted costs

11        should be recovered from each customer class. The embedded cost allocation study

12        provides information that should be reviewed and interpreted through the steps of

13        revenue distribution and rate design, but there is no requirement that it dictate all

14        aspects of revenue distribution and rates.

15               The proposed revenue distribution employs an approach that is often

16        referred to as gradualism. The use of gradualism appropriately balances increases

17        resulting from the CCOSS compared to current base rates with the goal of avoiding

18        an increase that could unduly affect the billing impact to customers. The use of a

19        gradualism approach also avoids the potential for over-correction due to variations

12             available to measure how the customer uses electricity. Residential customers, for

16             for streetlights are based on a per-light charge based upon the type of light and its

17             usage characteristics.

20             does not vary with monthly differences and that applies to each customer in a

21             customer class. The service availability charge generally recovers costs associated

 3   Q.   Please describe what a demand ratchet is and how it functions in utility rate

 4        structures.

 5   A.   A demand ratchet is a billing mechanism used in rate design for demand-billed

 6        customers. It sets the minimum billing demand for a given month at a specified

 7        percentage of the customer’s peak demand from a prior period, typically the highest

 8        demand in the preceding 11 months. This prevents dramatic fluctuations in bills

 9        due to seasonal or irregular usage patterns, promotes cost recovery stability for the

10        utility, and protects other customers from subsidizing under-recovery from

11        intermittent high-demand users. Demand costs are a function of a customer's annual

12        peak demand, and ratchets ensure recovery when monthly peaks fluctuate below

13        that level.

15   A.   Yes, SPS already has demand ratchets in place for its higher-voltage transmission

16        customers. Specifically, ratchets are included for rates applicable to customers

17        served at 69kV and above. These have been effective in maintaining equitable cost

18        allocation and revenue stability for those classes.

 2   A.   The current kVAR rate under-recovers the true system costs imposed by inefficient

 3        PF, as it does not sufficiently account for the use of the system. Poor PF increases

 4        apparent power (kVA) demand, leading to higher currents, greater losses, voltage

 5        regulation issues, and the need for oversized equipment across generation,

 6        transmission, and distribution (mentioned as relevant to other classes). Customers

 7        with low PF effectively use more system capacity than their kW demand suggests,

 8        shifting costs to efficient users. The existing rates are insufficient, often resulting

 9        in only modest charges (e.g., $100–$500/month for moderate excesses), which fail

10        to incentivize timely corrections like capacitor installations. By increasing the

11        kVAR rate, SPS is promoting fairness, enhancing grid efficiency, and aligning the

12        rate with cost causation principles without altering the commodity method

13        preferred by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission for transparency.

14   Q.   How did you calculate the proposed new kVAR rate for the LGS-T class?

15   A.   I derived a revised kVAR rate using a capacity-based benchmark applied to New

17        of summer and winter demand components). The formula for the revision is:

18           •   Revised kVAR Rate = Effective Demand Rate × (0.95 / Actual PF - 1) /

19               [tan(arccos(Actual PF)) - tan(arccos(0.95))]

20               Where tan(arccos(0.95)) ≈ 0.3286 (the threshold tangent).

 2   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony in this section?

 3   A.   I support SPS’s proposal for a Time-of-Use (TOU) fuel pilot program specifically

 4        for LGS-T customers in New Mexico. This pilot aims to introduce more accurate

 5        and time-differentiated price signals for fuel costs during the summer months,

 6        based on analysis of SPS’s total system load patterns and market dynamics.

 7   Q.   Can you describe the analytical basis for this proposed pilot?

 8   A.   Yes. The proposal is grounded in a load duration curve analysis, including a focused

 9        examination of the top 500 hours of system load. This analysis identifies significant

10        load ramps during certain summer hours, particularly in the Southwest Power Pool-

11        SPS load node, where peak demand can drive higher market settlement costs. These

12        ramps highlight price signals that can be used to better reflect the timing and

13        variability of costs incurred by the system.

14   Q.   Can you describe the existing FPPCAC fuel recovery mechanism in more

15        detail, including how it operates on a monthly basis?

16   A.   Yes. SPS's FPPCAC operates under NMPRC Rule 550 (17.9.550 NMAC) with a

17        monthly adjustment factor to flow through fuel and purchased power expenses per

18        kWh. Monthly fuel rates are set based on actual costs incurred on a two-month lag,

19        paired with forecasted sales volumes. For instance, actual costs from a given month

20        (e.g., August) are incorporated into the rate two months later (e.g., October), with


                                               77
                                    Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                   Alexander G. Trowbridge

1         true-ups in subsequent periods to reconcile any differences between actuals and

2         forecasts. All calculations are done on an average (non-time-differentiated) basis

3         across the system. This structure ensures that SPS collects only actual expended

4         costs while providing stability to revenues and cashflows during rising costs and

5         prompt credits during declines, but it inherently delays the reflection of costs in

6         customer bills, which can weaken price signals tied to real-time system conditions.

 7   Q.   What is SPS attempting to address when developing the LGS-T TOU Fuel

 8        Pilot?

 9   A.   The existing mechanism does not send a strong price signal to customers given that,

10        for example, actual fuel costs from August are passed through to customers in

11        October based on estimated October sales volumes rather than the actual conditions

12        during the high-cost period. This lag and estimation mismatch dilute the incentive

13        for customers to adjust usage in response to real-time system stresses, potentially

14        leading to inefficient resource utilization. The Fuel TOU pilot enhances this price

15        signal by reflecting higher prices during periods of increased load usage.

16   Q.   Why are accurate price signals important, and how might a forecasted price

17        approach help achieve that compared to the existing lagging method?

18   A.   First, it is important to note that SPS is not proposing a modification to the existing

19        FPPCAC mechanics as part of its TOU Fuel proposal. Rather, SPS’s TOU Fuel

20        proposal would function alongside the existing FPPCAC mechanism. That said,

                                                78

                                              of
                                   Alexander G. Trowbridge

1         accurate price signals are generally important because they align customer behavior

2         with actual system costs, encouraging efficient usage like load shifting away from

3         high-cost peaks, which can reduce overall system expenses, enhance grid

4         reliability, and promote fairness among customers. In volatile markets, timely

5         signals help customers make informed decisions on consumption and conservation.

6         Real-time prices send an accurate pricing signal but are administratively

7         burdensome to execute. A forecasted price approach, unlike the existing lagging

8         method, would provide prospective rates based on anticipated costs and volumes,

 9        allowing customers to respond proactively to expected high-cost periods rather than

10        reacting to lagged actuals. This could minimize mismatches between when costs

11        are incurred and when they are signaled, potentially leading to better load

12        management and lower long-term costs, though it requires robust forecasting to

13        maintain accuracy and would represent a shift from the current structure.

16        time-differentiated   rates—distinguishing    between    On-Peak     and    Off-Peak

17        periods—to better reflect historical settlement patterns in the Southwest Power

18        Pool-SPS load node. This approach will encourage load shifting away from high-

19        cost peak hours, aligning customer behavior more closely with system costs. The
